implementation_notes: TypeScript's most common metadata mapping: models are declared in the Prisma schema (field types, @id, @map("email_address"), @@map("users")) and the generated client exposes typed results; the entity is a plain type (or an interface derived from the generated type) and carries no runtime metadata at all. Because TS types are erased, the schema file is the only place the mapping exists - which is exactly the metadata-driven shape. Hand-written mapping in a repository remains the simpler replacement for raw-SQL paths, and decorator-based entities are the alternative variant.
pitfalls: Types are erased: nothing at runtime represents the entity, so validation/guards must come from the schema layer instead of the type.
Generated client types leak the storage shape into application code; wrap them in domain types if the schema must not become the contract.
The schema file is the source of truth: databases edited by hand drift from it until a migration is generated and applied.

variants.name: TypeORM decorator entities
variants.implementation_notes: Classic TS variant: the entity is a class annotated with @Entity/@PrimaryGeneratedColumn/@Column, with the metadata reflected at runtime through reflect-metadata, registered on the DataSource; the repository/manager performs persistence, so the class carries schema metadata but no queries. Choose it when a typed entity class is wanted and an external schema file is not acceptable.
pitfalls: Decorators need experimentalDecorators/emitDecoratorMetadata and a reflect-metadata import; without them the mapping is empty at runtime.
Property initialisers (id = 0) shadow persisted values in some configurations - use declare or definite assignment.
Repository methods make Active Record-style use tempting; keep those calls in a service/repository layer to preserve the separation.
